source: English: K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), public domain. Sanskrit: standard 700-verse text. Taxonomy: this project.

hexads.title: Hexad I - The Path of Action (Karma)
hexads.summary: From Arjuna's collapse on the battlefield to the discipline of selfless action and meditation: who we are (the immortal Self) and how to act without bondage.

hexads.title: Hexad II - The Path of Devotion (Bhakti)
hexads.summary: Krishna reveals his own nature: the source of all beings, the royal secret, his divine glories and the cosmic form, culminating in loving devotion as the most direct way.

hexads.title: Hexad III - The Path of Knowledge (Jnana)
hexads.summary: Analysis of matter and spirit, the three gunas, divine and demonic natures, faith, and finally the synthesis of renunciation, duty and surrender that ends Arjuna's doubt.

themes.name: Battlefield narrative
themes.description: The frame story at Kurukshetra: the armies, the warriors, conches blowing, Sanjaya reporting to Dhritarashtra.

themes.name: Arjuna's grief and moral crisis
themes.description: Arjuna's despair, compassion for kinsmen, fear of sin and refusal to fight; confusion about duty.

themes.name: The immortal Self (Atman)
themes.description: The soul is eternal, unborn and indestructible; bodies change like garments; do not grieve for what cannot die.

themes.name: Duty and one's own dharma
themes.description: Performing one's own duty according to one's nature and station; better one's own duty imperfectly done than another's well done.

themes.name: Selfless action (Karma Yoga)
themes.description: Acting without attachment to the fruits of action; work as an offering; action, inaction and wise action.

themes.name: Equanimity and the steady mind
themes.description: The person of steady wisdom, even-minded in pleasure and pain, success and failure, praise and blame; inner peace.

themes.name: Mind, senses, desire and anger
themes.description: Controlling the restless mind and the senses; desire and anger as the enemy; the chain from attachment to ruin.

themes.name: Sacrifice (Yajna) and offering
themes.description: Sacrifice as cosmic reciprocity; many forms of sacrifice; offering every act, food and gift to the divine.

themes.name: Knowledge and wisdom (Jnana)
themes.description: Spiritual knowledge that burns away karma; learning from the wise; discrimination between the real and unreal.

themes.name: Meditation and self-discipline (Dhyana)
themes.description: How to sit and meditate, moderation in food and sleep, steadying the mind like a lamp in a windless place.

themes.name: Devotion and surrender (Bhakti)
themes.description: Loving devotion to God, offering a leaf or flower with love, taking refuge, surrender, the qualities of a dear devotee.

themes.name: Krishna's divine nature and glories
themes.description: Krishna as the source and essence of all, his incarnations to restore righteousness, his higher and lower nature, his divine manifestations (vibhutis).

themes.name: The Universal Form (Vishvarupa)
themes.description: Arjuna's vision of the cosmic form of God with countless faces, blazing like a thousand suns, as all-devouring Time.

themes.name: Creation, death and rebirth
themes.description: Brahman, the cycles of creation and dissolution, days and nights of Brahma, remembering God at death, the paths of departure and rebirth.

themes.name: The three Gunas
themes.description: Sattva (goodness), rajas (passion) and tamas (inertia/darkness): how the qualities of nature bind, and how to transcend them.

themes.name: Field and knower; Prakriti and Purusha
themes.description: The body as the field, the Self as its knower; matter and spirit; the virtues that constitute knowledge; the imperishable Supreme Person.

themes.name: Divine and demonic qualities
themes.description: Fearlessness, purity, compassion versus hypocrisy, arrogance, anger, cruelty; lust, anger and greed as three gates to hell.

themes.name: Faith, food, austerity and charity
themes.description: Three kinds of faith, food, sacrifice, austerity and gifts according to the gunas; Om Tat Sat.

themes.name: Renunciation and liberation (Moksha)
themes.description: Sannyasa and tyaga, renouncing the fruits rather than action, the supreme secret of surrender, attainment of Brahman and freedom.

chapters.summary: The armies face each other at Kurukshetra. Duryodhana reviews the warriors, conches sound, and Arjuna asks Krishna to place the chariot between the armies. Seeing teachers, grandfathers and cousins ready to die, Arjuna is overwhelmed by grief and drops his bow.

Arjuna becomes Krishna's disciple. Krishna teaches the immortality of the Self, the warrior's duty, the discipline of action without attachment to results (2.47), and describes the person of steady wisdom whose mind is unmoved by pleasure and pain.

No one can remain without acting. Action done as sacrifice does not bind; the wise act to keep the world in order and set an example. Better one's own duty than another's. Desire and anger, born of rajas, are the real enemy.

chapters.name_english: Knowledge and the Renunciation of Action
chapters.summary: Krishna reveals the ancient lineage of this yoga and why he incarnates age after age (4.7-8). He explains action, inaction and wise action, lists many forms of sacrifice, and praises knowledge as the fire that burns all karma.

Renunciation and selfless action lead to the same goal, but action is easier. The yogi acts untouched like a lotus leaf on water, sees all beings with an equal eye, and finds joy within, reaching the peace of Brahman.

Raise yourself by yourself; the mind is friend or enemy. Practical instructions for meditation, moderation in eating and sleeping, the restless mind tamed by practice and detachment, and the reassurance that no sincere seeker is ever lost.

Krishna describes his lower eightfold nature and higher conscious nature; he is the taste in water and the light of sun and moon. His maya of the gunas is hard to cross; four kinds of people worship him, and the wise one is dearest.

Definitions of Brahman, adhyatma and karma. Whatever one remembers at death, one attains; so remember Krishna always. The cosmic days and nights of Brahma, and the two paths by which the departed do or do not return.

chapters.name_english: The Royal Knowledge and Royal Secret
chapters.summary: All beings rest in Krishna, yet he is beyond them. He is the father, mother, goal and refuge of the world. He accepts even a leaf, a flower, fruit or water offered with love, and devotion is open to everyone.

Krishna is the source of all; his devotees enjoy his presence and he gives them understanding. At Arjuna's request he names his chief manifestations - among lights the sun, among rivers the Ganga - and says all glory is a spark of his splendour.

chapters.name_english: The Vision of the Cosmic Form
chapters.summary: Given divine sight, Arjuna sees the universal form, radiant as a thousand suns, devouring the warriors. Krishna declares himself Time, the destroyer, and asks Arjuna to be his instrument. Terrified, Arjuna praises him and asks to see his gentle form again.

Devotion to the personal God is easier than meditation on the unmanifest. Krishna offers a ladder of practices and lists the qualities of the devotee dear to him: free from hatred, friendly, compassionate, even-minded and content.

The body is the field and the Self its knower. Humility, non-violence and other virtues are true knowledge. The supreme Brahman pervades all, and liberation comes from discerning Prakriti (matter) from Purusha (spirit).

Krishna is the seed-giving father of all beings. Sattva binds by attachment to happiness, rajas by attachment to action, tamas by delusion. One who goes beyond the three gunas through devotion attains immortality.

The world is an inverted ashvattha tree to be cut with detachment. A fragment of Krishna becomes the individual soul. He is the light in sun and fire and the digestive fire in beings - the Supreme Person beyond the perishable and imperishable.

Divine qualities lead to liberation, demonic ones to bondage. The demonic deny truth, live for desire and pride, and descend; lust, anger and greed are the triple gate to hell. Let scripture be the guide.
Each person's faith follows their nature. Food, sacrifice, austerity of body, speech and mind, and charity are each sattvic, rajasic or tamasic. Om Tat Sat sanctifies every act.

Renounce the fruits, not the duties. Knowledge, action, the doer, intellect, resolve and happiness are classified by the gunas. Doing one's own duty is worship. The supreme secret: abandon all and take refuge in Krishna (18.66). Arjuna's doubts are gone and he resolves to act.

sections.title: Duryodhana surveys the two armies
sections.label: BG 1.1-11
sections.text: [BG 1.1] Assembled together on the sacred plain of Kurukshetra from desire of fighting what did my sons and the Pandavas do, O Sanjaya. [BG 1.2] Beholding the army of the Pandavas arrayed, king Duryodhana, approaching the preceptor (Drona) said these words: [BG 1.3] Behold, O preceptor, this vast army of the son of Pandu, arrayed by Drupada's son (Dhrishtadyumna), thy intelligent disciple. [BG 1.4] There (in that army) are many brave and mighty bowmen, who in battle are equal to Bhima and Arjuna. [BG 1.5] (They are) Yuyudhana, and Virata, and that mighty car-warrior Drupada, and Dhrishtaketu, and Chekitana, and the ruler of Kasi endued with great energy; and Purujit, [BG 1.6] and Kuntibhoja, and Saivya that bull among men; and Yudhamanyu of great prowess, and Uttamaujas of great energy; and Subhadra's son, and the sons of Draupadi, all of whom are mighty car-warriors. [BG 1.7] Hear, however, O best of regenerate ones, who are the distinguished ones among us, the leaders of the army. I will name them to thee for (thy) information. [BG 1.8] (They are) thyself, and Bhishma, and Karna, and Kripa who is ever victorious; and Aswatthaman and Vikarna, and Saumadatta, and Jayadratha. [BG 1.9] Besides these, are many heroic warriors, prepared to lay down their lives for my sake, armed with diverse kinds of weapons, and all accomplished in battle. [BG 1.10] Our army, therefore, protected by Bhishma, is insufficient. This force, however, of these (the Pandavas), protected by Bhima, is sufficient. [BG 1.11] Stationing yourselves then in the entrances of the divisions that have been assigned to you, all of you protect Bhishma alone.'—(Just at this time) the valiant and venerable grandsire of the Kurus,

sections.title: The conches sound the call to battle
sections.label: BG 1.12-19
sections.text: [BG 1.12] affording great joy to him (Duryodhana) by loudly uttering a leonine roar, blew (his) conch. [BG 1.13] Then conches and drums and cymbals and horns were sounded at once and the noise (made) became a loud uproar. [BG 1.14] Then Madhava and Pandu's son (Arjuna), both stationed on a great car unto which were yoked white steeds, blew their celestial conches. [BG 1.15] And Hrishikesa blew (the conch called) Panchajanya and Dhananjaya (that called) Devadatta; and Vrikodara of terrible deeds blew the huge conch (called) Paundra. [BG 1.16] And Kunti's son king Yudhishthira blew (the conch called) Anantavijaya; while Nakula and Sahadeva, (those conches called respectively) Sughosa and Manipushpaka. [BG 1.17] And that splendid bowman, the ruler of Kasi and that mighty car-warrior, Sikhandin, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and that unvanquished Satyaki, [BG 1.18] and Drupada, and the sons of Draupadi, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadra—all these, O lord of earth, severally blew their conches. [BG 1.19] And that blare, loudly reverberating through the welkin, and the earth, rent the hearts of the Dhartarashtras.

sections.title: Arjuna looks upon his kinsmen
sections.label: BG 1.20-27
sections.text: [BG 1.20] Then beholding the Dhartarashtra troops drawn up, the ape-bannered son of Pandu, rising his bow, [BG 1.21] when, the throwing of missiles had just commenced, said these words, O lord of earth, to Hrishikesa. [BG 1.22] O thou that knoweth no deterioration, place my car (once) between the two armies, so that I may observe these that stand here desirous of battle, and with whom I shall have to contend in the labours of this struggle. [BG 1.23] I will observe those who are assembled here and who are prepared to fight for doing what is agreeable in battle to the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra. [BG 1.24] Thus addressed by Gudakesa, O Bharata, Hrishikesa, placing that excellent car between the two armies, [BG 1.25] in view of Bhishma and Drona and all the kings of the earth, said,—'Behold, O Partha these assembled Kurus,'—And there the son of Pritha beheld, [BG 1.26] standing (his) sires and grandsons, and friends, and father-in-law and well-wishers, in both the armies. [BG 1.27] Beholding all those kinsmen standing (there), the son of Kunti, possessed by excessive pity, despondingly said (these words).

sections.title: Arjuna's grief and arguments against the war
sections.label: BG 1.28-47
sections.text: [BG 1.28] Beholding these kinsmen, O Krishna, assembled together and eager for the fight, my limbs become languid, and my mouth becomes dry. [BG 1.29] My body trembles, and my hair stands on end. Gandiva slips from my hand, and my skin burns. [BG 1.30] I am unable to stand (any longer); my mind seems to wander. [BG 1.31] I behold adverse omens, too, O Kesava. I do not desire victory, O Krishna, not sovereignty, nor pleasures. [BG 1.32] Of what use would sovereignty be to us, O Govinda, or enjoyments, or even life, since they, for whose sake sovereignty, enjoyments, [BG 1.33] and pleasures are desired by us, are here arrayed for battle ready to give up life and wealth, [BG 1.34] viz., preceptors, sires, sons and grandsires, maternal uncles, father-in-laws, grandsons, brother-in-laws, and kinsmen. [BG 1.35] I wish not to slay these though they slay me, O slayer of Madhu, even for the sake of the sovereignty of the three worlds, what then for the sake of (this) earth? [BG 1.36] What gratification can be ours, O Janardana, by slaying the Dhartarashtras? Even if they be regarded as foes, sin will overtake us if we slay them. [BG 1.37] Therefore, it behoveth us not to slay the sons of Dhritarashtra who are our own kinsmen. How, O Madhava can we be happy by killing our own kinsmen? [BG 1.38] Even if these, with judgments perverted by avarice, do not see the evil that ariseth from the extermination of a race, [BG 1.39] and the sin of internecine quarrels, why should not we, O Janardana, who see the evils of the extermination of a race, learn to abstain from that sin? [BG 1.40] A race being destroyed, the eternal customs of that race are lost; and upon those customs being lost, sin overpowers the whole race. [BG 1.41] From the predominance of sin, O Krishna, the women of that race become corrupt. And the women becoming corrupt, an intermingling of castes happeneth, O descendant of Vrishni. [BG 1.42] This intermingling of castes leadeth to hell both the destroyer of the race and the race itself. The ancestors of those fall (from heaven), their rites of pinda and water ceasing. [BG 1.43] By these sins of destroyers of races, causing intermixture of castes, the rules of caste and the eternal rites of families become extinct. [BG 1.44] We have heard, O Janardana, that men whose family rites become extinct, ever dwell in hell. [BG 1.45] Alas, we have resolved to perpetrate a great sin, for we are ready to slay our own kinsmen from lust of the sweets of sovereignty. [BG 1.46] Better would it be for me if the sons of Dhritarashtra, weapon in hand, should in battle slay me (myself) unavenging unarmed. [BG 1.47] Having spoken thus on the field of battle, Arjuna, his mind troubled with grief, casting aside his bow and arrows, sat down on his car.

sections.title: Arjuna refuses to fight and becomes a disciple
sections.label: BG 2.1-10
sections.text: [BG 2.1] Unto him thus possessed with pity, his eyes filled and oppressed with tears, and desponding, the slayer of Madhu said these words. [BG 2.2] Whence, O Arjuna, hath come upon thee, at such a crisis, this despondency that is unbecoming a person of noble birth, that shuts one out from heaven, and that is productive of infamy? [BG 2.3] Let no effeminacy be thine, O son of Kunti. This suits thee not. Shaking off this vile weakness of hearts, arise, O chastiser of foes. [BG 2.4] How, O slayer of Madhu, can I with arrows contend in battle against Bhishma and Drona, deserving as they are, O slayer of foes, of worship? [BG 2.5] Without slaying (one's) preceptors of great glory, it is well (for one), to live on even alms in this world. By slaying preceptors, even if they are avaricious of wealth, I should only enjoy pleasures that are bloodstained! [BG 2.6] We know not which of the two is of greater moment to us, viz., whether we should conquer them or they should conquer us. By slaying whom we would not like to live,—even they, the sons of Dhritarashtra, stand before (us). [BG 2.7] My nature affected by the taint of compassion, my mind unsettled about (my) duty, I ask thee. Tell me what is assuredly good (for me). I am thy disciple. O, instruct me, I seek thy aid. [BG 2.8] I do not see (that) which would dispel that grief of mine blasting my very senses, even if I obtain a prosperous kingdom on earth without a foe or the very sovereignty of the gods. [BG 2.9] Having said this unto Hrishikesa, that chastiser of foes—Gudakesa—(once more) addressed Govinda, saying,—'I will not fight,'—and then remained silent. [BG 2.10] Unto him overcome by despondency, Hrishikesa, in the midst of the two armies, said:

sections.title: The Self is eternal: do not grieve
sections.label: BG 2.11-30
sections.text: [BG 2.11] Thou mournest those that deserve not to be mourned. Thou speakest also the words of the (so-called) wise. Those, however, that are (really) wise, grieve neither for the dead nor for the living. [BG 2.12] It is not that. I or you or those rulers of men never were, or that all of us shall not hereafter be. [BG 2.13] Of an Embodied being, as childhood, youth, and decrepitude are in this body, so (also) is the acquisition of another body. The man, who is wise, is never deluded in this. [BG 2.14] The contacts of the senses with their (respective) objects producing (sensations of) heat and cold, pleasure and pain, are not permanent, having (as they do) a beginning and an end. Do thou, O Bharata, endure them. [BG 2.15] For the man whom these afflict not, O bull among men, who is the same in pain and pleasure and who is firm in mind, is fit for emancipation. [BG 2.16] There is no (objective) existence of anything that is distinct from the soul; nor non-existence of anything possessing the virtues of the soul. [BG 2.17] This conclusion in respect of both these hath been arrived at by those that know the truths (of things). Know that the soul to be immortal by which all this universe is pervaded. [BG 2.18] No one can compass the destruction of that which is imperishable. It hath been said that those bodies of the Embodied (soul) which is eternal, indestructible and infinite, have an end. Do thou, therefore, fight, O Bharata. [BG 2.19] He who thinks it (the soul) to be the slayer and he who thinks it to be the slain, both of them know nothing; for it neither slays nor is slain. [BG 2.20] It is never born, nor doth it ever die; nor, having existed, will it exist no more. Unborn, unchangeable, eternal, and ancient, it is not slain upon the body being perished. [BG 2.21] That man who knoweth it to be indestructible, unchangeable, without decay, how and whom can he slay or cause to be slain? [BG 2.22] As a man, casting off robes that are worn out, putteth on others that are new, so the Embodied (soul), casting off bodies that are worn out, entereth other bodies that are new. [BG 2.23] Weapons cleave it not, fire consumeth it not; the waters do not drench it, nor doth the wind waste it. [BG 2.24] It is incapable of being cut, burnt, drenched, or dried up. It is unchangeable, all-pervading, stable, firm, and eternal. [BG 2.25] It is said to be imperceivable, inconceivable and unchangeable. Therefore, knowing it to be such, it behoveth thee not to mourn (for it). [BG 2.26] Then again even if thou regardest it as constantly born and constantly dead, it behoveth thee not yet, O mighty-armed one, to mourn (for it) thus. [BG 2.27] For, of one that is born, death is certain; and of one that is dead, birth is certain. Therefore it behoveth thee not to mourn in a matter that is unavoidable. [BG 2.28] All beings (before birth) were unmanifest. Only during an interval (between birth and death), O Bharata, are they manifest; and then again, when death comes, they become (once more) unmanifest. [BG 2.29] What grief then is there in this? One looks upon it as a marvel; another speaks of it as a marvel. Yet even after having heard of it, no one apprehends it truly. [BG 2.30] The Embodied (soul), O Bharata, is ever indestructible in everyone's body. Therefore, it behoveth thee not to grieve for all (those) creatures.

sections.title: The duty and honour of a warrior
sections.label: BG 2.31-38
sections.text: [BG 2.31] Casting thy eyes on the (prescribed) duties of thy order, it behoveth thee not to waver, for there is nothing else that is better for a Kshatriya than a battle fought fairly. [BG 2.32] Arrived of itself and (like unto) an open gate of heaven, happy are those Kshatriyas, O Partha, that obtain such a fight. [BG 2.33] But if thou dost not fight such a just battle, thou shalt then incur sin by abandoning the duties of thy order and thy fame. [BG 2.34] People will then proclaim thy eternal infamy, and to one that is held in respect, infamy is greater (as an evil) than death itself. [BG 2.35] All great car-warriors will regard thee as abstaining from battle from fear, and thou wilt be thought lightly by those that had (hitherto) esteemed thee highly. [BG 2.36] Thy enemies, decrying thy prowess, will say many words which should not be said. What can be more painful than that? [BG 2.37] Slain, thou wilt attain to heaven; or victorious, thou wilt enjoy the Earth. Therefore, arise, O son of Kunti, resolved for battle. [BG 2.38] Regarding pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat, as equal, do battle for battle's sake and sin will not be thine.

sections.title: Buddhi Yoga: action without attachment to results
sections.label: BG 2.39-53
sections.text: [BG 2.39] This knowledge, that hath been communicated to thee is (taught) in the Sankhya (system). Listen now to that (inculcated) in Yoga (system). Possessed of that knowledge, thou, O Partha, wilt cast off the bonds of action. [BG 2.40] In this (the Yoga system) there is no waste of even the first attempt. There are no impediments. Even a little of this (form of) piety delivers from great fear. [BG 2.41] Here in this path, O son of Kuru, there is only one state of mind, consisting in firm devotion (to one object, viz., securing emancipation). The minds of those, however, that are not firmly devoted (to this), are many-branched (un-settled) and attached to endless pursuits. [BG 2.42] That flowery talk which, they that are ignorant, they that delight in the words of the Vedas, they, O Partha, that say that there is nothing else, they whose minds are attached to worldly pleasures, [BG 2.43] they that regard (a) heaven (of pleasures and enjoyments) as the highest object of acquisition,—utter and promises birth as the fruit of action and concerns itself with multifarious rites of specific characters for the attainment of pleasures and power, [BG 2.44] delude their hearts and the minds of these men who are attached to pleasures and power cannot be directed to contemplation (of the divine being) regarding it as the sole means of emancipation. The Vedas are concerned with three qualities, (viz., religion, profit, and pleasure). [BG 2.45] Be thou, O Arjuna, free from them, unaffected by pairs of contraries (such as pleasure and pain, heat and cold, etc.), ever adhering to patience without anxiety for new acquisitions or protection of those already acquired, and self-possessed, whatever objects are served by a tank or well, [BG 2.46] may all be served by a vast sheet of water extending all around; so whatever objects may be served by all the Vedas, may all be had by a Brahmana having knowledge (of self or Brahma). [BG 2.47] Thy concern is with work only, but not with the fruit (of work). Let not the fruit be thy motive for work; nor let thy inclination be for inaction. [BG 2.48] Staying in devotion, apply thyself to work, casting off attachment (to it), O Dhananjaya, and being the same in success or unsuccess. This equanimity is called Yoga (devotion). [BG 2.49] Work (with desire of fruit) is far inferior to devotion, O Dhananjaya. Seek thou the protection of devotion. They that work for the sake of fruit are miserable. [BG 2.50] He also that hath devotion throws off, even in this world, both good actions and bad actions. Therefore, apply thyself to devotion. Devotion is only cleverness in action. [BG 2.51] The wise, possessed of devotion, cast off the fruit born of action, and freed from the obligation of (repeated) birth, attain to that region where there is no unhappiness. [BG 2.52] When thy mind shall have crossed the maze of delusion, then shalt thou attain to an indifference as regards the hearable and the heard. [BG 2.53] When thy mind, distracted (now) by what thou hast heard (about the means of acquiring the diverse objects of life), will be firmly and immovably fixed on contemplation, then wilt thou attain to devotion.

sections.title: The person of steady wisdom (sthitaprajna)
sections.label: BG 2.54-72
sections.text: [BG 2.54] What, O Kesava, are the indications of one whose mind is fixed on contemplation? How should one of steady mind speak, how sit, how move? [BG 2.55] When one casts off all the desires of his heart and is pleased within (his) self with self, then is one said to be of steady mind. [BG 2.56] He whose mind is not agitated amid calamities, whose craving for pleasure is gone, who is freed from attachment (to worldly objects), fear and wrath, is said to be a Muni of steady mind. [BG 2.57] His is steadiness of mind who is without affection everywhere, and who feeleth no exultation and no aversion on obtaining diverse objects that are agreeable and disagreeable. [BG 2.58] When one withdraws his senses from the objects of (those) senses as the tortoise its limbs from all sides, even his is steadiness of mind. [BG 2.59] Objects of senses fall back from an abstinent person, but not so the passion (for those objects). Even the passion recedes from one who has beheld the Supreme (being). [BG 2.60] The agitating senses, O son of Kunti, forcibly draw away the mind of even a wise man striving hard to keep himself aloof from them. [BG 2.61] Restraining them all, one should stay in contemplation, making me his sole refuge. For his is steadiness of mind whose senses are under control. [BG 2.62] Thinking of the objects of sense, a person's attachment is begotten towards them. [BG 2.63] From attachment springeth wrath; from wrath ariseth want of discrimination; from want of discrimination, loss of memory; from loss of memory, loss of understanding; and from loss of understanding (he) is utterly ruined. [BG 2.64] But the self-restrained man, enjoying objects (of sense) with senses freed from attachment and aversion under his own control, attaineth to peace (of mind). [BG 2.65] On peace (of mind) being attained, the annihilation of all his miseries taketh place, since the mind of him whose heart is peaceful soon becometh steady. [BG 2.66] He who is not self-restrained hath no contemplation (of self). He who hath no contemplation hath no peace (of mind). Whence can there be happiness for him who hath no peace (of mind)? [BG 2.67] For the heart that follows in the wake of the sense moving (among their objects) destroys his understanding like the wind destroying a boat in the waters. [BG 2.68] Therefore, O thou of mighty arms, his is steadiness of mind whose senses are restrained on all sides from the objects of sense. [BG 2.69] The restrained man is awake when it is night for all creatures; and when other creatures are awake that is night to a discerning Muni. [BG 2.70] He into whom all objects of desire enter, even as the waters enter the ocean which (though) constantly replenished still maintains its water-mark unchanged—(he) obtains peace (of mind) and not one that longeth for objects of desire. [BG 2.71] That man who moveth about, giving up all objects of desire, who is free from craving (for enjoyments) and who hath no affection and no pride, attaineth to peace (of mind). [BG 2.72] This, O Partha, is the divine state. Attaining to it, one is never deluded. Abiding in it one obtains, on death, absorption into the Supreme Self.

sections.title: Why act at all? No one can be without action
sections.label: BG 3.1-8
sections.text: [BG 3.1] If devotion, O Janardana, is regarded by thee as superior to work, why then, O Kesava, dost thou engage me in such dreadful work? [BG 3.2] By equivocal words thou seemest to confound my understanding. Therefore, tell (me) one thing definitely by which I may attain to what is good. [BG 3.3] It hath already been said by me, O sinless one, that here are, in this world, two kinds of devotion; that of the Sankhyas through knowledge and that of the yogins through work. [BG 3.4] A man doth not acquire freedom from work from (only) the non-performance of work. [BG 3.5] Nor doth he acquire final emancipation from only renunciation (of work). No one can abide even for a moment without doing work. [BG 3.6] That man of deluded soul who, curbing the organs of sense, liveth mentally cherishing the objects of sense, is said to be a dissembler. [BG 3.7] He however, O Arjuna, who restraining (his) senses by his mind, engageth in devotion (in the form) of work with the organs of work, and is free from attachment, is distinguished (above all). [BG 3.8] (Therefore), do thou always apply yourself to work, for action is better than inaction. Even the support of thy body cannot be accomplished without work.

sections.title: Action as sacrifice and the wheel of the world
sections.label: BG 3.9-16
sections.text: [BG 3.9] This world is fettered by all work other than that which is (performed) for Sacrifice. (Therefore), O son of Kunti, perform work for the sake of that, freed from attachment. [BG 3.10] In olden times, the Lord of Creation, creating men and sacrifice together, said,—flourish by means of this (Sacrifice). [BG 3.11] Let this (Sacrifice) be to you (all) the dispenser of all objects cherished by you. Rear the gods with this, and let the gods (in return) rear you. [BG 3.12] Thus fulfilling the mutual interest you will obtain that which is beneficial (to you). Propitiated with sacrifices the gods will bestow on you the pleasures you desire. [BG 3.13] He who enjoyeth (himself) without giving them what they have given, is assuredly a thief. The good who eat the remnant of sacrifices are freed from all sins. [BG 3.14] Those unrighteous ones incur sin who dress food for their own sake.—From food are all creatures; and sacrifice is the outcome of work. [BG 3.15] Know that work proceeds from the Vedas; Vedas have proceeded from Him who hath no decay. Therefore, the all-pervading Supreme Being is installed in sacrifice. [BG 3.16] He who conformeth not to this wheel that is thus revolving, that man of sinful life delighting (the indulgence of) his senses, liveth in vain, O Partha.

sections.title: The wise act to set an example
sections.label: BG 3.17-26
sections.text: [BG 3.17] The man, however, that is attached to self only, that is contented with self, and that is pleased in his self,—hath no work (to do). [BG 3.18] He hath no concern whatever with action nor with any omission here. Nor, amongst all creatures, is there any upon whom his interest dependeth. [BG 3.19] Therefore, always do work that should be done, without attachment. The man who performeth work without attachment, attaineth to the Supreme. [BG 3.20] By work alone, Janaka and others, attained the accomplishment of their objects. Having regard also to the observance by men of their duties, it behoveth thee to work. [BG 3.21] Whatever a great man doth, is also done by vulgar people. Ordinary men follow the ideal set by them (the great). [BG 3.22] There is nothing whatever for me, O Partha, to do in the three worlds, (since I have) nothing for me which hath not been acquired; still I engage in action. [BG 3.23] Because if at any time I do not, without sloth, engage in action, men would follow my path, O Partha, on all sides. [BG 3.24] The worlds would perish if I did not perform work, and I should cause intermixture of castes and ruin these people. [BG 3.25] As the ignorant work, O Bharata, having attachment to the performer, so should a wise man work without being attached, desiring to make men observant of their duties. [BG 3.26] A wise man should not cause confusion of understanding amongst ignorant persons, who have attachment to work itself; (on the other hand) he should (himself) acting with devotion engage them to all (kinds of) work.

sections.title: Nature acts; better one's own dharma
sections.label: BG 3.27-35
sections.text: [BG 3.27] All works are, in every way, done by the qualities of nature. He, whose mind is deluded by egoism, however, regards himself as the actor. [BG 3.28] But he, O mighty-armed one, who knoweth the distinction (of self) from qualities and work, is not attached to work, considering that it is his senses alone (and not his self) that engage in their objects. [BG 3.29] Those who are deluded by the qualities of nature, become attached to the works done by the qualities. A person of perfect knowledge should not bewilder those men of imperfect knowledge. [BG 3.30] Devoting all work to me, with (thy) mind directed to self, engage in battle, without desire, without affection and with thy (heart's) weakness dispelled. [BG 3.31] Those men who always follow this opinion of mine with faith and without cavil attain to final emancipation even by work. [BG 3.32] But they who cavil at and do not follow this opinion of mine, know, that, bereft of all knowledge and without discrimination, they are ruined. [BG 3.33] Even a wise man acts according to his own nature. All living beings follow (their own) nature. What then would restraint avail? [BG 3.34] The senses have, as regards the objects of the senses, either affection or aversion fixed. One should not submit to these, for they are obstacles in one's way. [BG 3.35] One's own duty, even if imperfectly performed, is better than being done by other even if well performed. Death in (performance of) one's own duty is preferable. (The adoption of) the duty of another carries fear (with it).

sections.title: Desire and anger: the real enemy
sections.label: BG 3.36-43
sections.text: [BG 3.36] Impelled by whom, O son of the Vrishni race, doth a man commit sin, even though unwilling and as if constrained by force? [BG 3.37] It is desire, it is wrath, born of the attribute of passion; it is all devouring, it is very sinful. [BG 3.38] Know this to be the foe in this world. As fire is enveloped by smoke, a mirror by dust, the foetus by the womb, so is this enveloped by desire. [BG 3.39] Knowledge, O son of Kunti, is enveloped by this constant foe of the wise in the form of desire which is insatiable and like a fire. [BG 3.40] The senses, the mind and the understanding are said to be its abode. With these it deludeth the embodied self, enveloping (his) knowledge. [BG 3.41] Therefore, restraining (thy) senses first, O bull of Bharata's race, cast off this wicked thing, for it destroyeth knowledge derived from instruction and meditation. [BG 3.42] It hath been said that the senses are superior (to the body which is inert). Superior to the senses is the mind. [BG 3.43] Superior to the mind is the knowledge. But which is superior to knowledge is He. Thus knowing that which is superior to knowledge and restraining (thy) self by self, slay, O mighty-armed one, the enemy in the shape of desire which is difficult to conquer.

sections.title: The ancient yoga and why Krishna incarnates
sections.label: BG 4.1-10
sections.text: [BG 4.1] This imperishable (system of) devotion I declared to Vivaswat; Vivaswat declared it to Manu; and Manu communicated it to Ikshaku. [BG 4.2] Descending thus from generation, the Royal sages came to know it. But, O chastiser of foes, by (lapse of a) long time that devotion became lost to the world. [BG 4.3] Even the same (system of) devotion hath today been declared by me to thee, for thou art my devotee and friend, (and) this is a great mystery. [BG 4.4] Thy birth is posterior; Vivaswat's birth is prior. How shall I understand then that thou hadst first declared (it)? [BG 4.5] Many births of mine have passed away, O Arjuna, as also of thine. These all I know, but thou dost not, O chastiser of foes. [BG 4.6] Though (I am) unborn and of essence that knoweth no deterioration, though (I am) the lord of all creatures, still, relying on my own (material) nature I take birth by my own (powers) of illusion. [BG 4.7] Whenever, O Bharata, loss of piety and the rise of impiety occurreth, on those occasions do I create myself. [BG 4.8] For the protection of the righteous and for the destruction of the evil doers, for the sake of establishing Piety, I am born age after age. [BG 4.9] He who truly knoweth my divine birth and work to be such, casting off (his body) is not born again; (on the other hand) he cometh to me, O Arjuna. [BG 4.10] Many who have been freed from attachment, fear, wrath, who were full of me, and who relied on me, have, cleansed by knowledge and asceticism, attained to my essence.

sections.title: All paths lead to Krishna; the four orders
sections.label: BG 4.11-15
sections.text: [BG 4.11] In whatsoever manner men come to me, in the selfsame manner do I accept them. It is my way, O Partha, that men follow on all sides. [BG 4.12] Those in this world who are desirous of the success of action worship the gods, for in this world of men success resulting from action is soon attained. [BG 4.13] The quadruple division of castes was created by me according to the distinction of qualities and duties. Though I am the author thereof, (yet) know me to be not their author and undecaying. Actions do not touch me. [BG 4.14] I have no longing for the fruits of actions. He that knoweth me thus is not impeded by actions. [BG 4.15] Knowing this, even men of old who were desirous of emancipation performed work. Therefore, do thou also perform work as was done by ancients of the remote past.

sections.title: Action, inaction and wise action
sections.label: BG 4.16-24
sections.text: [BG 4.16] What is action and what is inaction,—even the learned are perplexed at this. Therefore, I will tell thee about action (so that) knowing it thou mayst be freed from evil. [BG 4.17] One should have knowledge of action, and one should have knowledge of forbidden actions: one should also know of inaction. The course of action is incomprehensible. [BG 4.18] He, who sees inaction in action and action in inaction, is wise among men; he is possessed of devotion; and he is a doer of all actions. [BG 4.19] The learned call him wise whose efforts are all free from desire (of fruit) and (consequent) will, and whose actions have all been consumed by the fire of knowledge. [BG 4.20] Whoever, resigning all attachment to the fruit of action, is ever contented and is dependent on none, doth nought, indeed, although engaged in action. [BG 4.21] He who, without desire, with mind and the senses under control, and casting off all concerns, performeth action only for the preservation of the body, incurreth no sin. [BG 4.22] He who is contented with what is earned without exertion, who hath risen superior to the pairs of opposites, who is without jealousy, who is equable in success and failure, is not fettered (by action) even though he works. [BG 4.23] All his actions perish who acts for the sake of sacrifice, who is without affections, who is free (from attachments), and whose mind is fixed upon knowledge. Brahma is the vessel (with which the libation is poured); [BG 4.24] Brahma is the libation (that is offered); Brahma is the fire on which by Brahma is poured (the libation); Brahma is the goal to which he proceedeth by fixing his mind on Brahma itself which is the action.

sections.title: The many forms of sacrifice
sections.label: BG 4.25-33
sections.text: [BG 4.25] Some devotees perform sacrifice to the gods. Others, by means of sacrifice, offer up sacrifices to the fire of Brahma. Others offer up (as sacrificial libation) the senses of which hearing is the first to the fire of restraint. [BG 4.26] Others (again) offer up (as libations) the objects of sense of which sound is the first to the fire of the senses. [BG 4.27] Others (again) offer up all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital winds to the fire of devotion by self-restraint kindled by knowledge. [BG 4.28] Others again perform the sacrifice of wealth, the sacrifice of ascetic austerities, the sacrifice of meditation, the sacrifice of (Vedic) study, the sacrifice of knowledge, and others are ascetics of rigid vows. [BG 4.29] Some offer up the upward vital wind (Prana) to the downward vital wind (apana); and others, the downward vital wind to the upward vital wind; some, arresting the course of (both) the upward and the downward vital winds, are devoted to the restraint of the vital winds. [BG 4.30] Others of restricted rations, offer the vital winds to the vital winds. Even all these who are conversant with sacrifice, whose sins have been consumed by sacrifice, and who eat the remnants of sacrifice which are amrita, attain to the eternal Brahma. [BG 4.31] (Even) this world is not for him who doth not perform sacrifice. Whence then the other, O best of Kuru's race? [BG 4.32] Thus diverse are the sacrifices occurring in the Vedas. Know that all of them result from action, and knowing this thou wilt be emancipated. [BG 4.33] The sacrifice of knowledge, O chastiser of foes, is superior to every sacrifice involving (the attainment of) fruits of action, for all action, O Partha, is wholly comprehended in knowledge.

sections.title: The fire of knowledge burns all karma
sections.label: BG 4.34-42
sections.text: [BG 4.34] Learn that (Knowledge) by prostration, enquiry, and service. They who are possessed of knowledge and can see the truth, will teach thee that knowledge, knowing which, [BG 4.35] O son of Pandu, thou wilt not again come by such delusion, and by which thou wilt see the endless creatures (of the universe) in thyself (first) and then in me. [BG 4.36] Even if thou be the greatest sinner among all that are sinful, thou shalt yet cross over all transgressions by the raft of knowledge. [BG 4.37] As a blazing fire, O Arjuna, reduceth fuel to ashes, so doth the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes. [BG 4.38] For there is nothing here that is so cleansing as knowledge. One who hath attained to success by devotion finds it without effort within his own self in time. [BG 4.39] He obtaineth knowledge, who hath faith and is intent on it and who hath his senses under control; obtaining knowledge one findeth the highest tranquillity in no length of time. [BG 4.40] One who hath no knowledge and no faith, and whose minds is full of doubt, is lost. Neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness, is for him whose mind is full of doubt. [BG 4.41] Actions do not fetter him, O Dhananjaya, who hath cast off action by devotion, whose doubts have been dispelled by knowledge, and who is self-restrained. [BG 4.42] Therefore, destroying, by the sword of knowledge, this doubt of thine that is born of ignorance and that dwelleth in thy mind, betake to devotion, (and) arise, O son of Bharata.

sections.title: Renunciation and action lead to one goal
sections.label: BG 5.1-6
sections.text: [BG 5.1] Thou applaudest, O Krishna, the abandonment of actions, and again the application (to them). Tell me definitely which one of these two is superior. [BG 5.2] Both abandonment of actions and application to actions lead to emancipation. But of these, application to action is superior to abandonment. [BG 5.3] He should always be known to be an ascetic who hath no aversion nor desire. For, being free from pairs of opposites, O thou of mighty arms, he is easily released from the bonds (of action). [BG 5.4] Fools say, but not those that are wise, that Sankhya and Yoga are distinct. One who stayeth in even one (of the two) reapeth the fruit of both. [BG 5.5] Whatever seat is attained by those who profess the Sankhya system, that too is reached by those who profess the Yoga. He seeth truly who seeth Sankhya and Yoga as one. [BG 5.6] But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, without devotion (to action), is difficult to attain. The ascetic who is engaged in devotion (by action) reacheth the Supreme Being without delay.

sections.title: Acting untouched, like a lotus leaf on water
sections.label: BG 5.7-12
sections.text: [BG 5.7] He who is engaged in devotion (by action) and is of pure soul, who hath conquered his body and subdued his senses, and who indentifieth himself with all creatures, is not fettered though performing (action). [BG 5.8] The man of devotion, who knoweth truth, thinking—I am doing nothing—When seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, breathing, [BG 5.9] talking, excreting, taking, opening the eyelids or closing them; he regardeth that it is the senses that are engaged in the objects of senses. [BG 5.10] He who renouncing attachment engageth in actions, resigning them to Brahma, is not touched by sin as the lotus-leaf (is not touched) by water. [BG 5.11] Those who are devotees, casting off attachment, perform actions (attaining) purity of self, with the body, the mind, the understanding, and even the senses (free from desire). [BG 5.12] He who is possessed of devotion, renouncing the fruit of action, attaineth to the highest tranquillity. He, who is not possessed of devotion and is attached to the fruit of action, is fettered by action performed from desire.

sections.title: The equal vision of the wise
sections.label: BG 5.13-21
sections.text: [BG 5.13] The self-restrained embodied (self), renouncing all actions by the mind, remains at ease within the house of nine gates, neither acting himself nor causing (anything) to act. [BG 5.14] The Lord is not the cause of the capacity for action, or of the actions of men, or of the connection of actions and (their) fruit. [BG 5.15] It is nature that engages (in action). The Lord receiveth no one's sin, nor also merit. By ignorance, knowledge is shrouded. It is for this that creatures are deluded. [BG 5.16] But of whomsoever that ignorance hath been destroyed by knowledge of self, that knowledge (which is) like the Sun discloseth the Supreme Being. [BG 5.17] Those whose mind is on Him, whose very soul is He, who abide in Him, and who have Him for their goal, depart never more to return, their sins being all destroyed by knowledge. [BG 5.18] Those, who are wise cast an equal eye on a Brahmana endued with learning and modesty, on a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a chandala. [BG 5.19] Even here has birth been conquered by them whose minds rest on equality; and since Brahma is faultless and equable, therefore, they (are said to) abide in Brahma. [BG 5.20] He whose mind is steady, who is not deluded, who knows Brahma, and who rests in Brahma, doth not exult on obtaining anything that is agreeable, nor doth he grieve on obtaining that is disagreeable. [BG 5.21] He whose mind is not attached to external objects of sense, obtaineth that happiness which is in self; and by concentrating his mind on the contemplation of Brahma, he enjoyeth a happiness that is imperishable.

sections.title: Inner joy and the peace of Brahman
sections.label: BG 5.22-29
sections.text: [BG 5.22] The enjoyments born of the contact (of the senses with their objects) are productive of sorrow. He who is wise, O son of Kunti, never taketh pleasure in these that have a beginning and an end. [BG 5.23] That man whoever here, before the dissolution of the body, is able to endure the agitations resulting from desire and wrath, is fixed on contemplation, and is happy. [BG 5.24] He who findeth happiness within himself, (and) who sporteth within himself, he whose light (of knowledge) is deprived from within himself, is a devotee, and becoming one with Brahma attaineth to absorption into Brahma. [BG 5.25] Those saintly personages whose sins have been destroyed, whose doubts have been dispelled, who are self-restrained, and who are engaged in the good of all creatures, obtain absorption into Brahma. [BG 5.26] For these devotees who are freed from desire and wrath, whose minds are under control, and who have knowledge of self, absorption into Brahma exists both here and thereafter. [BG 5.27] Excluding (from his mind) all external objects of sense, directing the visual glance between the brows, mingling (into one) the upward and the downward life-breaths and making them pass through the nostrils, [BG 5.28] the devotee, who has restrained the senses, the mind, and the understanding, being intent on emancipation, and who is freed from desire, fear, and wrath, is emancipated, indeed. [BG 5.29] Knowing me to be enjoyer of all sacrifices and ascetic austerities, the great Lord of all the worlds, and friend of all creatures, such a one obtaineth tranquillity.

sections.title: Raise yourself by yourself
sections.label: BG 6.1-9
sections.text: [BG 6.1] Regardless of fruit of action, he that performs the actions which should be performed, is a renouncer and devotee, and not one who discards the (sacrificial) fire, nor one that abstains from action. [BG 6.2] That which has been called renunciation, know that, O son of Pandu, to be devotion, since nobody can be a devotee who has not renounced (all) resolves. [BG 6.3] To the sage desirous of rising to devotion, action is said to be the means; and when he has risen to devotion, cessation of action is said to be the means. [BG 6.4] When one is no longer attached to the objects of the senses, nor to actions, and when one renounces all resolves, then is one said to have risen to devotion. [BG 6.5] One should raise (his) self by self; one should not degrade (his) self; for one's own self is one's friend, and one's own self is one's enemy. [BG 6.6] To him (only) who has subjugated his self by his self is self a friend. But to him who has not subjugated his self, his self behaves inimically like an enemy. [BG 6.7] The soul of one who has subjugated his self and who is in the enjoyment of tranquillity, is steadily fixed (on itself) amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and also honour and dishonour. [BG 6.8] That ascetic is said to be devoted whose mind is satisfied with knowledge and experience, who hath no affection, who hath subjugated his senses, and to whom a sod, a stone and gold are alike. [BG 6.9] He, who views equally well-wishers, friends, foes, strangers that are indifferent to him, those who take part with both sides,

sections.title: How to sit in meditation; moderation
sections.label: BG 6.10-17
sections.text: [BG 6.10] those who are objects of aversion, those who are related (to him), those who are good, and those who are wicked, is distinguished (above all others). [BG 6.11] A devotee should always fix his mind on contemplation, remaining in a secluded place alone, restraining both mind and body, without expectations (of any kind), and without concern (with anything). [BG 6.12] Erecting his seat immovably on a clean spot, not too high nor too low, and spreading over it a piece of cloth, a deer-skin, or blades of Kusa grass, and there seated on that seat, with mind fixed on one object, and restraining the functions of the heart and the senses, one should practise contemplation for the purification of self. [BG 6.13] Holding body, head, and neck even, unmoved and steady, and casting his glance on the tip of his nose, and without looking about in any of the different directions, [BG 6.14] with mind in tranquillity, freed from fear, observant of the practices of Brahmacharins, restraining the mind, with heart fixed on me, the devotee should sit down, regarding me as the object of his attainment. [BG 6.15] Thus applying his soul constantly, the devotee whose heart is restrained, attains to that tranquillity which culminates in final absorption and assimilation with me. [BG 6.16] Devotion is not one's, O Arjuna, who eateth much, nor one's who doth not eat at all; nor one's who is addicted to too much sleep, [BG 6.17] nor one's who is always awake, devotion that is destructive of misery is his who is temperate in food and amusements, who duly exerts himself temperately in all his works, and who is temperate in sleep and vigils.

sections.title: The perfected yogi: a lamp in a windless place
sections.label: BG 6.18-32
sections.text: [BG 6.18] When one's heart, properly restrained, is fixed on one's own self, then, indifferent to all objects of desire, he is one called a devotee. [BG 6.19] As a lamp in a windless spot doth not flicker, even that is the resemblance declared of a devotee whose heart hath been restrained and who applieth his self to abstraction. [BG 6.20] That (condition) in which the mind, restrained by practice of abstraction, taketh rest, in which beholding self by self, [BG 6.21] one is gratified within self; in which one experienceth that highest felicity which is beyond the (sphere of the) senses and which the understanding (only) can grasp, and fixed on which one never swerveth from the truth; acquiring which one regards no other acquisition greater than it, [BG 6.22] and abiding in which one is never moved by even the heaviest sorrow; that (Condition) should be known to be what is called devotion in which there is a severance of connection with pain. [BG 6.23] That devotion should be practised with perseverance and with an undesponding heart. [BG 6.24] Renouncing all desires without exception that are born of resolves, restraining the group of the senses on all sides by mind alone, [BG 6.25] one should, by slow degrees, become quiescent (aided) by (his) understanding controlled by patience, and then directing his mind to self should think of nothing. [BG 6.26] Wheresoever the mind, which is (by nature) restless and unsteady, may run, restraining it from those, one should direct it to self alone. [BG 6.27] Indeed, unto such a devotee whose mind is in tranquillity, whose passions have been suppressed, who hath become one with Brahma and who is free from sin, the highest felicity cometh (of his own accord). [BG 6.28] Thus applying his soul constantly (to abstraction), the devotee, freed from sin, easily obtaineth that highest happiness, viz., with Brahma. [BG 6.29] He who hath devoted his self to abstraction casting an equal eye everywhere, beholdeth his self in all creatures and all creatures in his self. [BG 6.30] Unto him who beholdeth me in everything and beholdeth everything in me, I am never lost and he also is never lost to me. [BG 6.31] He who worshippeth me as abiding in all creatures, holding yet that all is one, is a devotee, and whatever mode of life he may lead, he liveth in me. [BG 6.32] That devotee, O Arjuna, who casteth an equal eye everywhere, regarding all things as his own self and the happiness and misery of others as his own, is deemed to be the best.

sections.title: Taming the restless mind
sections.label: BG 6.33-36
sections.text: [BG 6.33] This devotion by means of equanimity which thou hast declared, O slayer of Madhu,—on account of restlessness of the mind I do not see its stable presence. [BG 6.34] O Krishna, the mind is restless, boisterous, perverse, and obstinate. Its restraint I regard to be as difficult of accomplishment as the restraint of the wind. [BG 6.35] Without doubt, O thou of mighty arms the mind is difficult of subjugation and is restless. With practice, however, O son of Kunti, and with the abandonment of desire, it can be controlled. [BG 6.36] It is my belief that by him whose mind is not restrained, devotion is difficult of acquisition. But by one whose mind is restrained and who is assiduous, it is capable of acquisition with the aid of means.

sections.title: No sincere seeker is ever lost
sections.label: BG 6.37-47
sections.text: [BG 6.37] Without assiduity, though endued with faith, and with mind shaken off from devotion, what is the end of him, O Krishna, who hath not earned success in devotion? [BG 6.38] Fallen off from both, is he lost like a separated cloud or not, being as he is without refuge, O thou of mighty arms, and deluded on the path leading to Brahma? [BG 6.39] This my doubt, O Krishna, it behoveth thee to remove without leaving anything. Besides thee, no dispeller of this doubt is to be had. [BG 6.40] O son of Pritha, neither here, nor hereafter, doth ruin exist for him, since none, O sire, who performs good (acts) comes by an evil end. [BG 6.41] Attaining to the regions reserved for those that perform meritorious acts and living there for many many years, he that hath fallen off from devotion taketh birth in the abode of those that art pious and endued with prosperity, [BG 6.42] or, he is born even in the family of devotees endued with intelligence. Indeed, a birth such as this is more difficult of acquisition in this world. [BG 6.43] There in those births he obtaineth contact with that Brahmic knowledge which was his in his former life; and from that point he striveth again, O descendant of Kuru, towards perfection. [BG 6.44] And although unwilling, he still worketh on in consequence of that same former practice of his. Even one that enquireth of devotion riseth above (the fruits of) the Divine Word. [BG 6.45] Striving with great efforts, the devotee, cleaned of all his sins, attaineth to perfection after many births, and then reacheth the supreme goal. [BG 6.46] The devotee is superior to ascetics engaged in austerities; he is esteemed to be superior to even the man of knowledge. The devotee is superior to those that are engaged in action. [BG 6.47] Therefore, become a devotee, O Arjuna. Even amongst all the devotees, he who, full of faith and with inner self resting on me, worshippeth me, is regarded by me to be the most devout.

sections.title: Krishna's lower and higher nature
sections.label: BG 7.1-7
sections.text: [BG 7.1] Listen, O son of Pritha, how, without doubt, thou mayst know me fully, fixing thy mind on me, practising devotion, and taking refuge in me. [BG 7.2] I will now, without leaving anything out speak to thee about knowledge and experience, knowing which there would be left nothing in this world (for thee) to know. [BG 7.3] One among thousands of men striveth for perfection. Of those even that are assiduous and have attained to perfection, only some one knoweth me truly. [BG 7.4] Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, also understanding, and consciousness,—thus hath my nature been divided eight-fold. This is a lower (form of my) nature. [BG 7.5] Different from this, know there is a higher (form of my) nature which is animate, O thou of mighty arms, and by which this universe is held. [BG 7.6] Know that all creatures have these for their source. I am the source of evolution and also of the dissolution of the entire universe. [BG 7.7] There is nothing else, O Dhananjaya, that is higher than myself. Upon me is all this like a row of pearls on a string.

sections.title: Krishna as the essence of all things
sections.label: BG 7.8-12
sections.text: [BG 7.8] Taste I am in the waters, O son of Kunti, (and) I am the splendour of both the moon and the sun, I am the Om in all the Vedas, the sound in space, and the manliness in men. [BG 7.9] I am the fragrant odour in earth, the splendour in fire, the life in all (living) creatures, and penance in ascetics. [BG 7.10] Know me, O son of Pritha, to be the eternal seed of all beings. I am the intelligence of all creatures endued with intelligence, the glory of all glorious objects. [BG 7.11] I am also the strength of all that are endued with strength, (myself) freed from desire and thirst, and, O bull of Bharata's race, am the desire, consistent with duty, in all creatures. [BG 7.12] And all existences which are of the quality of goodness, and which are of the quality of passion and quality of darkness, know that they are, indeed, from me.

sections.title: Maya and the four kinds of devotees
sections.label: BG 7.13-19
sections.text: [BG 7.13] I am, however, not in them, but they are in me. This entire universe, deluded by these three entities consisting of (these) three qualities knoweth not me that am beyond them and undecaying; since this illusion of mine, [BG 7.14] depending on the (three) qualities, is exceedingly marvellous and highly difficult of being transcended. They that resort to me alone cross this illusion. [BG 7.15] Doers of evil, ignorant men, the worst of their species, robbed of their knowledge by (my) illusion and wedded to the state of demons, do not resort to me. [BG 7.16] Four classes of doers of good deeds worship me, O Arjuna, viz., he that is distressed, that is possessed of knowledge, being always devoted and having his faith in only One, [BG 7.17] is superior to the rest, for unto the man of knowledge I am dear above everything, and he also is dear to me. All these are noble. [BG 7.18] But the man of knowledge is regarded (by me) to be my very self, since he, with soul fixed on abstraction, taketh refuge in me as the highest goal. [BG 7.19] At the end of many births, the man possessed of knowledge attaineth to me, (thinking) that Vasudeva is all this. Such a high-souled person, however, is exceedingly rare.

sections.title: Worship of other gods and knowing the Supreme
sections.label: BG 7.20-30
sections.text: [BG 7.20] They who have been robbed of knowledge by desire, resort to their godheads, observant of diverse regulations and controlled by their own nature. [BG 7.21] Whatever form, (of godhead or myself) any worshipper desireth to worship with faith, that faith of his unto that (form) I render steady. [BG 7.22] Endued with that faith, he payeth his adorations to that (form), and obtaineth from that all his desire, since all those are ordained by me. [BG 7.23] The fruits, however, of those persons endued with little intelligence are perishable. They that worship the divinities, go to the divinities, (while) they that worship me come even to me. [BG 7.24] They that have no discernment, regard me who am (really) unmanifest to have become manifest, because they do not know the transcendent and undecaying state of mine than which there is nothing higher. [BG 7.25] Shrouded by the illusion of my inconceivable power, I am not manifest to all. This deluded world knoweth not me that I am unborn and undecaying. [BG 7.26] I know, O Arjuna, all things that have been past, and all things that are present, and all things that are to be. But there is nobody that knoweth me. [BG 7.27] All creatures, O chastiser of foes, are deluded at the time of their birth by the delusion, O Bharata, of pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion. [BG 7.28] But those persons of meritorious deeds whose sins have attained their end, being freed from the delusion of pairs of opposites, worship me, firm in their vow (of that worship). [BG 7.29] Those who, taking refuge in me, strive for release from decay and death, know Brahman, the entire Adhyatma, and action. [BG 7.30] And they who know me with the Adhibhuta, the Adhidaiva, and the Adhiyajna, having minds fixed on abstraction, know me at the time of their departure (from this world).

sections.title: Brahman, adhyatma and karma defined
sections.label: BG 8.1-4
sections.text: [BG 8.1] What is that Brahman, what is Adhyatma, what is action, O best of male beings? What also has been said to be Adhibhuta, and what is called Adhidaiva? [BG 8.2] Who is here Adhiyajna, and how, in this body, O slayer of Madhu? And how at the time of departure art thou to be known by those that have restrained their self'? [BG 8.3] Brahman is the Supreme and indestructible. Adhyatma is said to be its own manifestation. [BG 8.4] The offering (to any godhead in a sacrifice) which causeth the production and development of all—this is called action.

sections.title: Remembering Krishna at the hour of death
sections.label: BG 8.5-16
sections.text: [BG 8.5] Remembering me alone in (his) last moments, he that, casting off his body, departeth (hence), cometh into my essence. There is no doubt in this. [BG 8.6] Whichever form (of godhead) one remembereth when one casteth off, at the end, (his) body, unto that one he goeth, O son of Kunti, having habitually meditated on it always. [BG 8.7] Therefore, think of me at all times, and engage in battle. Fixing thy mind and understanding on me, thou wilt, without doubt, come even to me. [BG 8.8] Thinking (of the Supreme) with a mind not running to other objects and endued with abstraction in the form of uninterrupted application, one goeth, O son of Pritha, unto the Divine and Supreme male Being. [BG 8.9] He who at the time of his departure, with a steady mind, endued with reverence, with power of abstraction, and directing the life-breath called Prana between the eye-brows, thinketh of that ancient seer, who is the ruler (of all), [BG 8.10] who is minuter than the minutest atom, who is the ordainer of all, who is inconceivable in form, and who is beyond all darkness, cometh unto that Divine and Supreme Male Being. [BG 8.11] I will tell thee in brief about that seat which persons conversant with the Vedas declare to be indestructible, which is entered by ascetics freed from all longings, and in expectation of which (people) practise the vows of Brahmacharins. [BG 8.12] Casting off (this) body, he who departeth, stopping up all the doors, confining the mind within the heart, placing his own life-breath called Prana between the eye-brows, [BG 8.13] resting on continued meditation, uttering this one syllable Om which is Brahman, and thinking of me, attaineth to the highest goal. [BG 8.14] He who always thinketh of me with mind ever withdrawn from all other objects, unto that devotee always engaged on meditation, I am, O Partha, easy of access. [BG 8.15] High-souled persons who have achieved the highest perfection, attaining to me, do not incur re-birth which is the abode of sorrow and which is transient. [BG 8.16] All the worlds, O Arjuna, from the abode of Brahman downwards have to go through a round of births; on attaining to me, however, O son of Kunti, there is no re-birth.

sections.title: Days and nights of Brahma
sections.label: BG 8.17-22
sections.text: [BG 8.17] They who know a day of Brahman to end after a thousand Yugas, and a night (of his) to terminate after a thousand Yugas are persons that know day and night. [BG 8.18] On the advent of (Brahman's) day everything that is manifest springeth from the unmanifest; and when (his) night cometh, into that same which is called unmanifest all things disappear. [BG 8.19] That same assemblage of creatures, springing forth again and again, dissolveth on the advent of night, and springeth forth (again), O son of Pritha, when day cometh, constrained (by the force of action, etc.). [BG 8.20] There is, however, another entity, unmanifest and eternal, which is beyond that unmanifest, and which is not destroyed when all the entities are destroyed. [BG 8.21] It is said to be unmanifest and indestructible. They call it the highest goal, attaining which no one hath to come back. That is my Supreme seat. [BG 8.22] That Supreme Being, O son of Pritha, He within whom are all entities, and by whom all this is permeated, is to be attained by reverence undirected to any other object.

sections.title: The two paths of departure
sections.label: BG 8.23-28
sections.text: [BG 8.23] I will tell thee the times, O bull of Bharata's race, in which devotees departing (from this life) go, never to return, or to return. [BG 8.24] The fire, the Light, the day, the lighted fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice, departing from here, the persons knowing Brahma go through this path to Brahma. [BG 8.25] Smoke, night, also the dark-fortnight (and) the six months of the southern solstice, (departing) through this path, devotee, attaining to the lunar light, returneth. [BG 8.26] The bright and the dark, these two paths, are regarded to be the eternal (two paths) of the universe. By the one, (one) goeth never to return; by the other, one (going) cometh back. [BG 8.27] Knowing these two paths, O son of Pritha, no devotee is deluded. Therefore, at all times, be endued with devotion, O Arjuna. [BG 8.28] The meritorious fruit that is prescribed for the (study of the) Vedas, for sacrifices, for ascetic austerities and for gifts, a devotee knowing all this (that hath been said here), attaineth to it all, and (also) attaineth the Supreme and Primeval seat.

sections.title: The royal secret: all beings rest in Krishna
sections.label: BG 9.1-10
sections.text: [BG 9.1] Now I will tell thee that art without envy that most mysterious knowledge along with experience, knowing which thou wilt be freed from evil. [BG 9.2] This is royal science, a royal mystery, highly cleansing, directly apprehensible, consistent with the sacred laws, easy to practise, (and) imperishable. [BG 9.3] Those persons, O chastiser of foes, who have no faith in this sacred doctrine, not attaining to me, return to the path of this world that is subject to destruction. [BG 9.4] This entire universe is pervaded by me in my unmanifest form. All entities are in me, but I do not reside in them. [BG 9.5] Nor yet are all entities in me. Behold my divine power. Supporting all entities and producing all entities, myself doth not (yet) reside in (those) entities. [BG 9.6] As the great and obiquitious atmosphere always occupieth space, understand that all entities reside in me in the same way. [BG 9.7] All entities, O son of Kunti, attain to my nature at the close of a Kalpa. I create them again at the beginning of a Kalpa. [BG 9.8] Regulating my own (independent) nature I create again and in this whole assemblage of entities which is plastic in consequence of its subjection to nature. [BG 9.9] Those acts, however, O Dhananjaya, do not fetter me who sitteth as one unconcerned, being unattached to those acts (of creation). [BG 9.10] Through me, the overlooker, primal nature produceth the (universe of) mobiles and immobiles. For the reason, O son of Kunti, the universe passeth through its rounds (of birth and destruction).

sections.title: The deluded and the great-souled; Krishna as all
sections.label: BG 9.11-19
sections.text: [BG 9.11] Not knowing my supreme nature of the great lord of all entities, ignorant people of vain hopes, vain acts, [BG 9.12] vain knowledge, confounded minds, wedded to the delusive nature of Asuras and Rakshasas, disregard me (as one) that hath assumed a human body. [BG 9.13] But high-souled ones, O son of Pritha, possessed of divine nature, and with minds directed to nothing else, worship me, knowing (me) to be the origin of all entities and undestructible. [BG 9.14] Always glorifying me, (or) striving with firm vows, (or) bowing down to me, with reverence and ever devoted, (they) worship me. [BG 9.15] Others again, performing the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me, (some) as one, (some) as distinct, (some) as pervading the universe, in many forms. [BG 9.16] I am the Vedic sacrifice, I am the sacrifice enjoined in the Smritis, I am Swadha, I am the medicament produced from herbs; I am the mantra, I am the sacrificial libation, I am the fire, and I am the (sacrificial) offering. [BG 9.17] I am the father of this universe, the mother, the creator, grandsire; (I am) the thing to be known, the means by which everything is cleaned, the syllable Om, the Rik, the Saman and the Yajus, [BG 9.18] (I am) the goal, the supporter, the lord, the on-looker, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the source, the destruction, the support, the receptacle, and the undestructible seed. [BG 9.19] I give heat, I produce and suspend rain; I am immortality, and also death; and I am the existent and the non-existent, O Arjuna.

sections.title: Ritual for heaven versus devotion
sections.label: BG 9.20-25
sections.text: [BG 9.20] They who know the three branches of knowledge, also drink the Soma juice, and whose sins have been cleansed worshipping me by sacrifices, seek admission into heaven; and these attaining to the sacred region of the chief of the gods, enjoy in heaven the celestial pleasure of the gods. [BG 9.21] Having enjoyed that celestial world of vast extent, upon exhaustion of their merit they re-enter the mortal world. It is thus that they who accept the doctrines of the three Vedas and wish for objects of desires, obtain going and coming. [BG 9.22] Those persons who, thinking (of me) without directing their minds to anything else, worship me, of those who are (thus) always devoted (to me)—I make them gifts and preserve what they have. [BG 9.23] Even those devotees who, endued with faith, worship other godheads, even they, O son of Kunti, worship me alone, (though) irregularly. [BG 9.24] I am the enjoyer, as also the lord, of all sacrifices. They, however, do not know me truly; hence they fall off (from heaven). [BG 9.25] They whose vows are directed to the Pitris attain to the Pitris; who direct (their) worship to the inferior spirits called Bhutas attain to Bhutas; they who worship me, attain even to myself.

sections.title: A leaf, a flower, a fruit: devotion open to all
sections.label: BG 9.26-34
sections.text: [BG 9.26] They who offer me with reverence, leaf, flower, fruit, water—that offered with reverence, I accept from him whose self is pure. [BG 9.27] Whatever thou dost, whatever eatest, whatever drinkest, whatever givest, whatever austerities thou performest, manage it in such a way, O son of Kunti, that it may be an offering to me. [BG 9.28] Thus mayst thou be freed from the fetters of action having good and evil fruits. With self endued with renunciation and devotion, thou wilt be released and will come to me. [BG 9.29] I am alike to all creatures; there is none hateful to me, none dear. They, however, who worship me with reverence are in me and I also am in them. [BG 9.30] If even a person of exceedingly wicked conduct worshippeth me, without worshipping any one else, he should certainly be regard as good, for his efforts are well-directed. [BG 9.31] (Such a person) soon becometh of virtuous soul, and attaineth to eternal tranquillity. Know, O son of Kunti, that none devoted to me is ever lost. [BG 9.32] For, O son of Pritha, even they who may be of sinful birth, women, Vaisyas, and also Sudras, even they, resorting to me, attain to the supreme goal. [BG 9.33] What then (shall I say) of holy Brahmanas and saints who are my devotees? Having come to this transient and miserable world, be engaged in my worship. [BG 9.34] Fix thy mind on me; be my devotee, my worshipper; bow to me; and thus making me thy refuge and applying thy self to abstraction, thou wilt certainly come to me.

sections.title: Krishna, source of all; the joy of devotees
sections.label: BG 10.1-11
sections.text: [BG 10.1] Once more still, O mighty-armed one, listen to my supernal words which, from desire of (thy) good, I say unto thee that wouldst be pleased (therewith). [BG 10.2] The hosts of gods know not my origin, nor the great Rishis, since I am, in every way, the source of the gods and the great Rishis. [BG 10.3] He that knoweth me as the Supreme Lord of the worlds, without birth and beginning, (he), undeluded among mortals, is free from all sins. [BG 10.4] Intelligence, knowledge, the absence of delusion, forgiveness, truth, self-restraint, and tranquillity, pleasure, pain, birth, death, fear, and also security, abstention from harm, [BG 10.5] evenness of mind, contentment, ascetic austerities, gift, fame, infamy, these several attributes of creatures arise from me. [BG 10.6] The Seven great Rishis, the four Maharishis before (them), and the Manus, partaking of my nature, were born from my mind, of whom in this world are these offsprings. [BG 10.7] He that knoweth truly this pre-eminence and mystic power of mine, becometh possessed of unswerving devotion. Of this (there is) no doubt. [BG 10.8] I am the origin of all things, from me all things proceed. Thinking thus, the wise, endued with my nature, worship me. [BG 10.9] Their hearts on me, their lives devoted to me, instructing one another, and glorifying me they are ever contented and happy. [BG 10.10] Unto them always devoted, and worshipping (me) with love, I give that devotion in the form of knowledge by which they come to me. [BG 10.11] Of them, for compassion's sake, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance, by the brilliant lamp of knowledge, (myself) dwelling in their souls.

sections.title: Arjuna asks to hear the divine glories
sections.label: BG 10.12-18
sections.text: [BG 10.12] Thou art the Supreme Brahma, the Supreme Abode, the Holiest of the Holy, the eternal Male Being Divine, the First of gods Unborn, the Lord. [BG 10.13] All the Rishis proclaim thee thus, and also the celestial Rishi Narada; and Asita, Devala, (and) Vyasa; thyself also tellest me (so). [BG 10.14] All this that thou tellest me, O Kesava, I regard as true since, O Holy One, neither the gods nor the Danavas understand thy manifestation. [BG 10.15] Thou only knowest thyself by thyself. O Best of Male Beings, O Creator of all things; [BG 10.16] O Lord of all things, O God of gods, O Lord of the Universe, it behoveth thee to declare without any reservation, those divine perfections of thine by which perfections pervading these worlds thou abidest. [BG 10.17] How shall I, ever meditating, know thee, O thou of mystic powers, in what particular states mayst thou, O Holy One, be meditated upon by me? [BG 10.18] Do thou again, O Janardana, copiously declare thy mystic powers and (thy) perfections, for I am never satiated with hearing thy nectar-like words.

sections.title: The divine manifestations (vibhutis)
sections.label: BG 10.19-42
sections.text: [BG 10.19] Well, unto thee I will declare my divine perfections, by means of the principal ones (among them), O chief of the Kurus, for there is no end to the extent of my (perfections). [BG 10.20] I am the soul, O thou of curly hair, seated in the heart of every being, I am the beginning, and the middle, and the end also of all beings. [BG 10.21] I am Vishnu among the Adityas, the resplendent Sun among all luminous bodies; I am Marichi among the Maruts, and the Moon among constellations. [BG 10.22] I am the Sama Veda among the Vedas; I am Vasava among the gods; I am the mind among the senses; I am the intellect in (living) beings. [BG 10.23] I am Sankara among the Rudras, the Lord of treasures among the Yakshas and the Rakshasas; I am Pavaka among the Vasus, and Meru among the peaked (mountains). [BG 10.24] Know me, O son of Pritha, to be Vrihaspati, the chief of household priests. I am Skanda among commanders of forces. I am Ocean among receptacles of water. [BG 10.25] I am Bhrigu among the great Rishis, I am the One, undestructible (syllable Om) among words. Of sacrifices I am the Japa-sacrifice. Of immobiles I am the Himavat. [BG 10.26] I am the figtree among all trees, I am Narada among the celestial Rishis. I am Chitraratha among the Gandharvas and the ascetic Kapila among ascetics crowned with Yoga success.
